subject: Quantitative Aptitude
topic: Profit and loss V — mixed tiers
description: P&L: discounts, marked price, successive discounts, dishonest dealers

questions.stem: An article is sold for ₹720 at 20% loss. Cost price is:
questions.explanation: When LOSS is x%, SP = CP × (1 − x/100). So 720 = CP × 0.80 → CP = 900. Verify: 20% of 900 = 180; 900 − 180 = 720 ✓. KEY INSIGHT — work backwards using SP/CP factors: GAIN of x% → factor (1 + x/100); LOSS of x% → factor (1 − x/100). Common SSC trap: students directly compute 720 + 20% = 864 (option C) — that adds 20% of SP, not CP. Always anchor percentage to BASE (here, CP). GENERAL FORMULA: CP = SP × 100/(100 − loss%) for loss; CP = SP × 100/(100 + gain%) for gain.

questions.stem: Marked price ₹500. Successive discounts of 10% and 20% are given. Final selling price is:
questions.explanation: Successive discounts NEVER simply add. After 10% off: 500 × 0.9 = 450. After 20% off: 450 × 0.8 = 360. NET DISCOUNT FORMULA for two successive discounts a, b: a + b − (ab/100) = 10 + 20 − 200/100 = 28%. So SP = MP × (1 − 28/100) = 500 × 0.72 = 360. INSIGHT — order doesn't matter (multiplication is commutative); 10% then 20% = 20% then 10% = 28% net. CLASSIC TRAP: students add to get 30% (= 350) — option A. Retailers exploit this: 'Buy 1 get 50% off on 2nd' sounds like 50% but is really 25% on the pair. RELATED: successive % CHANGE formula (gain/loss) = a + b + ab/100 (with sign).

questions.stem: A dealer marks goods 25% above CP and gives 10% discount. His profit % is:
questions.explanation: Assume CP = 100 (always pick CP=100 for % problems). MP = 125 (25% above CP). SP after 10% discount = 125 × 0.9 = 112.5. Profit = 12.5 on CP of 100 → 12.5%. SHORTCUT FORMULA: net % = mark-up + discount + (mark-up × discount)/100 with appropriate signs = 25 + (−10) + 25(−10)/100 = 25 − 10 − 2.5 = 12.5%. INSIGHT — markup % + discount % don't simply subtract, because their bases differ (markup on CP, discount on MP). REAL-WORLD: this is exactly how retail works — high markup + 'attractive discount' = healthy margin. SSC PYQ favourite.

questions.stem: Selling 8 articles for ₹100 results in 20% loss. To gain 25%, the SP of 8 articles should be:
questions.explanation: Step 1 — find CP: SP at 20% loss = 80% of CP → 100 = 0.8 × CP → CP = 125 for 8 articles. Step 2 — new SP at 25% gain = 125 × 1.25 = 156.25 for 8 articles. INSIGHT — TWO-STEP method always works: first reverse-engineer CP from given (SP, %), then forward-compute desired SP from (CP, target %). SHORTCUT: new SP = old SP × (100 + target%)/(100 − loss%) = 100 × 125/80 = 156.25. CP per article = 15.625; new SP per article = 19.53. Useful in inventory pricing where cost is known but target margin changes.

questions.stem: By selling at ₹450 a man gains 12.5%. To gain 25%, he must sell at:
questions.explanation: 450 = (1 + 12.5/100) × CP = 1.125 × CP → CP = 400. New SP at 25% gain = 400 × 1.25 = 500. SHORTCUT: new SP = old SP × (100 + new gain%)/(100 + old gain%) = 450 × 125/112.5 = 500. INSIGHT — when old + new are both PROFITS, you can directly scale SP by the ratio of (1 + gain%) factors. KEY: never mix base; CP must be the anchor. PYQ trick: students compute 450 × 1.25 = 562.5 (option C/D ballpark) — they apply 25% on SP not CP. Always reduce to CP first.

questions.stem: A dishonest dealer claims to sell at cost but uses 800 g weight for a kg. His profit % is:
questions.explanation: DISHONEST DEALER FORMULA: gain % = [(true weight − false weight) / false weight] × 100 = (1000−800)/800 × 100 = 25%. WHY: he charges customer for 1 kg but actually delivers 800 g. He effectively SELLS 800 g for the cost-price of 1000 g → gains the cost of 200 g, on his actual COST of 800 g → 25%. COMMON MISTAKE: dividing by 1000 (true weight) gives 20% — wrong because dealer's cost was for 800 g actually delivered. EXTENSION: if dealer also marks up % above CP, total gain compounds. BALANCE-FRAUD QUESTIONS test whether you know the BASE = false weight, not true weight.

questions.stem: If CP of 12 articles equals SP of 9 articles, gain percent is:
questions.explanation: 12 CP = 9 SP → SP/CP = 12/9 = 4/3. Gain = (SP − CP)/CP = (4/3 − 1)/1 = 1/3 = 33⅓%. SHORTCUT FORMULA: when 'CP of x = SP of y', gain% = ((x − y)/y) × 100 if x > y (gain), or loss% = ((y − x)/x) × 100 if y > x (loss). Here x=12, y=9 → (12−9)/9 = 33.33%. INSIGHT: this ratio framework lets you skip plugging actual numbers. EXAMPLE 2: if SP of 5 = CP of 4 → loss% = (5−4)/5 × 100 = 20%. SSC + banking PYQ pattern.

questions.stem: A trader earns a profit that is exactly 20% of his selling price on every transaction. What is his actual profit percentage calculated on cost price?
questions.explanation: Let SP = 100. Profit = 20% of SP = 20. So CP = 80. Profit% on CP = (20/80)×100 = 25%. Option B (20%) is wrong because profit expressed as a percentage of SP is always lower than the same profit expressed as a percentage of CP; the two rates coincide only when profit = 0.

questions.stem: A manufacturer sells to a distributor at 20% profit; the distributor sells to a retailer at 10% profit; the retailer sells to the customer at 25% profit. If the manufacturer's cost price is ₹100, how much does the final customer pay?

options.option_text: ₹155 — all three margins added directly to base
₹132 — only two markups applied in the supply chain
₹165 — compounding of all three successive markups
₹180 — distributor's margin taken at 20% instead of 10%

questions.explanation: Each markup compounds on the previous price: 100 × 1.20 × 1.10 × 1.25 = 165. Option A (₹155) is wrong because it naively adds percentages (20+10+25 = 55%), ignoring that each stage's markup is calculated on the already-marked-up price, not the original ₹100.

questions.stem: A shopkeeper sells one-third of his stock at a 15% loss. At what profit percentage must he sell the remaining two-thirds so that he earns an overall profit of 5% on the entire stock?
questions.explanation: Let total CP = 3k. SP from loss lot = 0.85k. Required total SP for 5% gain = 3.15k. SP needed from remaining 2k lot = 3.15k − 0.85k = 2.30k, so profit = 0.30k on CP 2k → 15%. Option A (20%) is wrong — it assumes recovery needed = 15+5 = 20%, ignoring that the remaining lot is twice as large, so it absorbs the shortfall more efficiently.

questions.stem: Two articles A and B together cost ₹2,000. Article A is sold at 30% profit and Article B at 20% loss, yielding an overall gain of ₹50. What is the cost price of Article A?

options.option_text: ₹1,000 as cost price of Article A
₹900 as cost price of Article A
₹800 as cost price of Article A
₹1,100 as cost price of Article A

questions.explanation: Let CP_A = x, CP_B = 2000−x. Equation: 0.3x − 0.2(2000−x) = 50 → 0.5x = 450 → x = 900. Option A (₹1,000) is wrong — an equal split gives a net gain of 0.3×1000 − 0.2×1000 = ₹100, not ₹50, proving A's share must be smaller. Option D (₹1,100) is the CP of B, arising from swapping which article is at profit vs loss.

questions.stem: A merchant buys goods worth ₹8,000, then spends ₹400 on transportation and ₹600 on packaging. He wants 15% profit on his total outlay. At what price should he sell the goods?

options.option_text: ₹10,350 — profit on total cost including all overheads
₹9,200 — profit on ₹8,000 purchase price, overheads ignored
₹10,200 — overhead added separately after profit markup
₹9,660 — profit on purchase and transport, packaging excluded

questions.explanation: Total outlay = 8000+400+600 = ₹9,000. SP = 9000 × 1.15 = ₹10,350. Option B (₹9,200) is wrong — it computes 8000×1.15, treating only the purchase price as cost; all overheads are part of total outlay and must be included before the 15% margin is applied.

questions.stem: A dishonest dealer uses a 1,200 g weight in place of 1 kg while buying goods, and an 800 g weight in place of 1 kg while selling. If he transacts at the stated price per kg throughout, what is his overall profit percentage?

options.option_text: 25% — only the selling-side fraud is accounted for
40% — both fraud margins are added linearly
20% — only the buying-side fraud is accounted for
50% — compounding effect of buying and selling frauds

questions.explanation: Over LCM(1200,800) = 2400 g: dealer buys 2400 g by paying for 2×1000 = 2000 g worth (CP = ₹2,000); sells 2400 g by charging for 3×1000 = 3000 g worth (SP = ₹3,000). Profit = ₹1,000/₹2,000 = 50%. Option B (40%) is wrong — it adds (1200−1000)/1000 + (1000−800)/1000 = 20+20 = 40%; but the two frauds multiply: effective gain ratio = (1200/1000) × (1000/800) = 3/2, giving 50%.

questions.stem: A trader has 500 articles with a total cost price of ₹10,000. He sells 300 articles at 25% profit. At what price per article must he sell each of the remaining 200 articles to earn an overall profit of 20% on the entire lot?

options.option_text: ₹25 per article — same rate as first lot sold
₹22.50 per article on the remaining 200 items
₹24 per article — 20% profit applied per item

questions.explanation: CP per article = ₹10,000/500 = ₹20. Revenue from 300 at 25% profit = 300×25 = ₹7,500. Required total revenue for 20% profit on ₹10,000 = ₹12,000. Revenue needed from 200 remaining = 12,000−7,500 = ₹4,500; SP = 4500/200 = ₹22.50. Option D (₹24) is wrong — it applies 20% to individual CP (20×1.2 = 24), ignoring that the above-target profit on the first lot lowers the required selling price on the second.
